papers.title: A systematic comparison of physics-informed neural networks and mechanistic models for epidemic modeling and forecasting
papers.abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have recently been applied to epidemic modeling and forecasting with promising results. These methods integrate mechanistic knowledge with data-driven learning. Yet, their comparative performance against well-established, and simpler epidemic models is underexplored. Here, we conduct a systematic comparison of a PINN-based framework and a stochastic mechanistic model. Both approaches share the same age-structured SEIRD core and rolling-window forecasting pipeline, in a deliberately minimal setting. We evaluate their retrospective fits and probabilistic forecasts in two synthetic scenarios and the first COVID-19 wave in London. Interestingly, while PINNs underperform in synthetic scenarios, they achieve better performance on real data. Furthermore, PINNs provide narrower uncertainty intervals and sharper estimation of parameters in synthetic scenarios. Our findings confirm PINNs as a promising tool in epidemiology. At the same time, the results reaffirm the value of simpler approaches such as traditional compartmental models, and promote additional benchmarking studies.

papers.title: Latent resonances in oscillator networks
papers.abstract: In networks of coupled oscillators, from neural circuits to power grids, damping is expected to suppress oscillations because of its dissipativity. Here we show that local damping can, counterintuitively, amplify oscillations along some input-output channels, while the network's global oscillation energy decreases and its spectral properties improve. The amplified oscillation arises from a latent resonance that lies in the spectrum yet barely manifests. The added passive damping reshapes this resonance by mixing it with adjacent eigenmodes. In random power-grid networks, damping can boost weakly responding channels by more than an order of magnitude, while subdominant channels can grow to exceed the originally strongest channel. Damping thus not only suppresses oscillations but also provides a way to redistribute oscillatory energy. For any passive network, the amplified response and its upper bound follow exactly from baseline quantities, offering a principled route for network design and control.

papers.title: Match classification in the last round of four-team round-robin tournaments
papers.abstract: Classification of matches played in the last rounds of sports competitions is a well-established tool for evaluating tournament designs. Our paper offers the first comparison of deterministic and probabilistic match classification models by analysing the most prominent example of four-team round-robin competitions, the group stage of the FIFA World Cup. We show that both models are highly relevant in practice: all (four) deterministic and (six) probabilistic match types occurred in the 2014 and 2018 FIFA World Cups, respectively. The probabilistic model, which accounts for the relative benefits of attacking and defending, provides a deeper insight; for instance, the competitive matches from the deterministic approach can be of any of the six probabilistic types. Therefore, the probabilistic model is used to decompose the impact of three reforms introduced in the 2026 FIFA World Cup: the expansion to 48 teams, the modified qualification rules, and head-to-head tie-breakers.

papers.title: Spatial scaling of heterogeneity transfer from boron concentration to absorbed dose in boron neutron capture therapy
papers.abstract: We investigate how the amplitude and spatial correlation length of boron-concentration fluctuations affect the boron-induced absorbed-dose distribution in boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT). The spatial energy-deposition response of alpha particles and lithium nuclei is obtained using Geant4 and convolved with three-dimensional correlated lognormal boron fields under a uniform neutron field. Approximately $90\%$ of the reaction-product energy is deposited within a radius of $6.00~\mu\mathrm{m}$, with a characteristic deposition length of $\ell_B\approx2.05~\mu\mathrm{m}$. Dose heterogeneity increases with both the fluctuation amplitude $H$ and correlation length $\xi$, while the transfer factor $S=CV_D/H$ exhibits an approximate scaling collapse as a function of $\xi/\ell_B$. Analytical Gaussian and lognormal--Gaussian models provide reference predictions for this behavior. At short correlation lengths, the Geant4 response yields a higher transfer factor than a Gaussian response with the same characteristic length, highlighting the influence of the energy-deposition shape on dose smoothing. For $D_{95}$, defined as the dose received by at least $95\%$ of the modeled volume, the relative difference between homogeneous and heterogeneous boron-dose models reaches $(86.62\pm1.07)\%$ at $H=1.2$ and a target ratio $\xi/\ell_B=6$. We show that mean boron concentration alone is insufficient to characterize spatial nonuniformity of the boron-dose component.

papers.title: The directions of science: How we search the unknown
papers.abstract: Science is producing knowledge at unprecedented scale, while artificial intelligence promises to accelerate the generation of hypotheses, analyses, and scientific outputs further. Yet increasing the volume of research does not necessarily expand the range of directions science effectively explores. We argue that science can be understood as a collective search process in which finite resources are allocated across an evolving space of possible research trajectories. Careers, funding, organization, publication, attention, and technology act as interacting selection mechanisms that shape this allocation. This Perspective distinguishes the visible diversity of scientific activity from its effective diversity: apparently different researchers, institutions, or projects need not provide genuinely different routes of exploration or evaluation. Our principal contribution is to introduce cross-stage dependence, which occurs when selection processes operating at different stages of science are not fully independent in the grounds through which they favour scientific trajectories. We hypothesize that, under uncertainty, repeated filtering through overlapping criteria, information, prior selections, or technological infrastructure can reduce the capacity of science to maintain plausible alternatives and redirect effort when evidence changes their relative promise. Artificial intelligence makes this problem increasingly consequential because it can simultaneously expand scientific search capacity and participate across multiple stages of production and selection. The challenge is therefore not simply to produce more knowledge, but to preserve sufficiently distinct routes of exploration, verification and correction while retaining the ability to change direction.

papers.title: Learning Dynamics of the Influencer's Game in Resource Landscapes
papers.abstract: Across domains as varied as ecology, economics, and online platforms, individuals are incentivized to position themselves within resource-rich strategy spaces. In this work we introduce a new spatial game framework called the influencer's game. Within this new framework players' strategies are represented as positions within a trait space. Players then receive a share of a portion of a resource based on their relative influence at that resource's points traits. For the influencer's game, we show that there is a unique symmetric Nash equilibrium that exists under strict log-concavity of the influence kernel. Using the unique equilibrium we show that the stability of the system depends on the influence kernel's parameters, number of players, and the resource distribution shape. For any dimension we demonstrate a stability threshold that depends on both the scatter and curvature of the players. When this threshold is crossed, the symmetric equilibrium destabilizes and gives way to a variety of bifurcation types; including, specialist clusters, limit cycles, and sub-games that reproduce the larger game's structure. We ground these results using real-world data for resources as a demonstration of the game's application. Finally we extend the game dynamics to use multi-agent reinforcement learning and further show that the predicted bifurcation structure persists under partial observability and discretized strategy spaces. In all, the influencer's game provides a novel framework for predicting when competitive pressure drives convergence versus fragmentation with possible applications across domains.
